claims.source: The percentages of cells in Figure 1E, H showed that, in general, the outer menisci had higher cell type diversities.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cell type composition analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: In the more diverse outer menisci, the degenerated group had higher immune cell ratios and lower ACTA2+ cell ratios.
claims.source: In the more diverse outer menisci, the degenerated group (A1, B2, and D2) had higher immune cell ratios and lower ACTA2+ cell ratios.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cell type composition analysis.

claims.claim: Cell clusters were identified as chondrocytes if they expressed a high level of cartilage-related genes such as DCN, PRG4, COL1A2, COL3A1, ACAN, COMP, FN1, CHI3L1, and CHI3L2.
claims.source: We identified cell clusters as chondrocytes if they expressed a high level of cartilage-related genes such as DCN, PRG4, COL1A2, COL3A1, ACAN, COMP, FN1, CHI3L1, and CHI3L2.
claims.evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying chondrocytes based on marker gene expression.

claims.claim: Cell clusters with high expression levels of PLVAP and PECAM1 were identified as endothelial cells.
claims.source: We identified cell clusters with high expression levels of PLVAP, PECAM1 as endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying endothelial cells based on marker gene expression.

claims.claim: Immune cells were identified using high PTPRC, myeloid markers CD68, C1QA, HLA-DQA1, and T cell markers CD3D, CD3E.
claims.source: Immune cells were identified using high PTPRC, myeloid markers CD68, C1QA, HLA-DQA1, and T cell markers CD3D, CD3E.
claims.evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying immune cells based on marker gene expression.

claims.claim: A group of cells separated from other cells in both inner and outer areas of the meniscus has high expression levels of ACTA2 and was tentatively named 'pericyte-like cells' or PCL.
claims.source: In addition, there are a group of cells separated from other cells in both inner and outer areas of the meniscus, which has high expression levels of ACTA2. Besides high expressions of ACTA2, this group of cells also expressed some chondrocyte-associated gene markers, such as COL1A2, COL3A1, DCN, and FN1. We tentatively named this ACTA2+ group 'pericyte-like cells' or PCL (Figure 1I, J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B) and reanalyzed them together with the chondrocytes in Figure 2 and associated texts.
claims.evidence: This describes the identification and naming of a novel cell population based on marker expression.

claims.claim: Five chondral clusters named chondrocyte-1 to chondrocyte-5 (Ch.1–Ch.5) and two pericyte-like cell clusters (PCL.1 and PCL.2) were identified.
claims.source: We finally identified five chondral clusters named chondrocyte-1 to chondrocyte-5 (Ch.1–Ch.5 in Figure 2A) and two pericyte-like cell clusters (PCL.1 and PCL.2 in Figure 2A) named ACTA2+ cells in Figure 1D, G.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the hierarchical cell type classification.

claims.claim: Common fibroblast markers like DCN and LUM are highly expressed in the chondral class.
claims.source: Common fibroblast markers like DCN and LUM are highly expressed in the chondral class.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the marker gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Smooth muscle cell and pericyte markers like ACTA2, TAGLN, and MYL9 are highly expressed in the PCL class.
claims.source: Smooth muscle cell and pericyte markers like ACTA2, TAGLN, and MYL9 are highly expressed in the PCL class.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the marker gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: The PCL cells present strong muscle contractile gene expression signatures including ACTA2, MYL9, TAGLN.
claims.source: The PCL cells present strong muscle contractile gene expression signatures (Figure 2F), including ACTA2, MYL9, TAGLN, etc.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: ACTA2 encodes a smooth muscle actin involved in vascular contractility.
claims.source: ACTA2, which encodes a smooth muscle actin involved in vascular contractility, as well as TAGLN (transgelin) and MYH/MYL (myosin heavy/light chains) genes.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of ACTA2.

claims.claim: ACTA2, TAGLN, and MYH/MYL genes have been used for identifying pericytes or smooth muscle cells across multiple human organs.
claims.source: These genes have been used for identifying pericytes or smooth muscle cells across multiple human organs, including intervertebral disc (Gan et al., 2021), intestinal tract (Elmentaite et al., 2021), heart (Litvinukova et al., 2020), brain (Smyth et al., 2018), etc.
claims.evidence: This references multiple studies that have used these markers for cell identification.

claims.claim: Gene set enrichment analyses of PCL signature genes suggested the PCL population has a discrepant molecular identity from the chondrocyte lineage.
claims.source: The gene set enrichment analyses of these signature genes suggested the PCL population has a discrepant molecular identity from the chondrocyte lineage because GO terms such as 'muscle contraction', 'muscle organ development', and 'smooth muscle cell proliferation' were enriched (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the gene set enrichment analysis results.

claims.claim: Sun et al., 2020 named a similar ACTA2+ MYLK+ MCAM+ MYL9+ cluster as the FCP and claimed FCP could differentiate into degenerated meniscus progenitors (DegP) in degenerated menisci.
claims.source: In the work of Sun et al., 2020, they named a similar ACTA2+ MYLK+ MCAM+ MYL9+cluster as the FCP and claimed FCP could differentiate into degenerated meniscus progenitors (DegP) in degenerated menisci, or into adipogenic/osteogenic lineages when cultured ex vivo.
claims.evidence: This references findings from Sun et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The PCL population in the current study showed weak differentiation potential into DegP because this group of cells did not show concentrated expressions of DegP markers GREM1, CDCP1, and DNER.
claims.source: We did not name the population we found as FCP for three reasons: Firstly, enrichment analyses showed its similarity to pericytes/smooth muscle cells. Secondly, our PCL population showed weak differentiation potential into DegP because this group of cells in our data did not show concentrated expressions of DegP markers GREM1, CDCP1, and DNER.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the marker gene expression analysis comparing to Sun et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The PCL cells are more abundant in the vascularized outer meniscus region than in the avascular inner part.
claims.source: The PCL cells are more abundant in the vascularized outer meniscus region than in the avascular inner part (Figure 1E, H).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cell composition analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence imaging found that PCL cells lay around the vascular endothelial cells and formed a tube shape outside the blood vessels.
claims.source: Our immunofluorescence imaging found that this population of cells lay around the vascular endothelial cells and formed a tube shape outside the blood vessels (Figure 4A, B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Gan et al., 2021 named a group of ACTA2+ MCAM+ TAGLN+ cells in the human intervertebral disc as pericytes.
claims.source: Gan et al., 2021 named a group of ACTA2+ MCAM+ TAGLN+ in the human intervertebral disc as pericytes, which can be a reference for defining meniscal cell clusters.
claims.evidence: This references findings from Gan et al., 2021 on intervertebral disc cell types.

claims.claim: It is difficult to fully distinguish pericyte from smooth muscle cells purely based on the transcriptomes because the two cell types share numerous markers.
claims.source: We admit that it is difficult to fully distinguish pericyte from smooth muscle cells purely based on the transcriptomes because the two cell types share numerous markers, and their markers appear to be dynamic and affected by the tissue types and pathogenic states (van Dijk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Pericytes attach to the surface of vascular endothelial cells and maintain vasculature stability via the endothelium–pericyte crosstalk.
claims.source: It is known that pericytes attach to the surface of vascular endothelial cells and maintain vasculature stability via the endothelium–pericyte crosstalk (Eilken et al., 2017; Sugihara et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte function, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Pericytes have pro-angiogenesis capabilities.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that pericytes have pro-angiogenesis capabilities (Eilken et al., 2017; Armulik et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte function, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Both PCL.1 and PCL.2 expressed ECM components Collagen IVα1 (COL4A1), Collagen IVα2 (COL4A2), and Collagen XVIII (COL18A1), the non-collagenous fragments of which were known to have anti-angiogenesis functions.
claims.source: For example, in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, we showed that both PCL.1 and PCL.2 expressed ECM components Collagen IVα1 (COL4A1), Collagen IVα2 (COL4A2), and Collagen XVIII (COL18A1), the non-collagenous fragments of which (i.e., arresten, canstatin, and endostatin, respectively) were known to have anti-angiogenesis functions (de Castro Brás and Frangogiannis, 2020; Marneros and Olsen, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Two subtle subclusters were identified within the PCL class: PCL.1 expresses a higher level of FABP4, RGS5, and PCL.2 has relatively higher expressions of MYH11, MYH9, CNN1, and TAGLN.
claims.source: We identified two subtle subclusters within the PCL class. One subcluster PCL.1 expresses a higher level of FABP4, RGS5, and the other PCL.2 subcluster has relatively higher expressions of MYH11, MYH9, CNN1, and TAGLN.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the subclustering analysis of PCL cells.

claims.claim: Kumar et al., 2017 analyzed FABP4, RGS5, MYH11, MYH9, CNN1, and TAGLN genes' functions in the specification and diversification of pericyte/smooth muscle cells from mesenchymoangioblasts.
claims.source: Kumar et al., 2017 analyzed these genes' functions in the specification and diversification of pericyte/smooth muscle cells from mesenchymoangioblasts.
claims.evidence: This references findings from Kumar et al., 2017 on pericyte/smooth muscle cell differentiation.

claims.claim: PCL.1 had more active responses to the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and TNF-α.
claims.source: The GSVA suggested that PCL.1 had more active responses to the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and TNF-α (Figure 2G) and expressed higher levels of chemokines genes CCL2, CCL19, CCL21, CXCL12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), and COL4A1/2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: PCL.2 had higher myofibril gene set activation scores, indicating this population could have higher muscle contractility and may regulate the blood flow in the microvasculature.
claims.source: The GSVA scores suggested that PCL.2 had higher myofibril gene set activation scores, indicating this population could have higher muscle contractility and may regulate the blood flow in the microvasculature (van Dijk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis, with functional interpretation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The largest chondrocyte branch is the chondrocyte-1 (Ch.1) population that highly expresses CHAD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, ECRG (C2orf40), and APOD.
claims.source: The largest branch is the chondrocyte-1 (Ch.1) population that highly expresses CHAD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, ECRG (C2orf40), and APOD.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claims.claim: Some Ch.1 marker genes (e.g., CHI3L1/2) have been described as the markers of RegC.
claims.source: Some of these genes (e.g., CHI3L1/2) have been described as the markers of RegC (Ji et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This references findings from Ji et al., 2019 on regulatory chondrocyte markers.

claims.claim: Ch.1 cluster's percentage decreased in the degeneration group.
claims.source: This cluster's percentage decreased in the degeneration group.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cell composition analysis.

claims.claim: Gene set activation analysis indicated that Ch.1 population had anti-angiogenesis effects.
claims.source: The gene set activation analysis indicated that this population of cells had anti-angiogenesis effects (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Ch.1 highly expressed ECM regulators TIMP1 and TIMP4, which were inhibitors of ECM destruction proteins.
claims.source: ECM-related gene expressions indicated Ch.1 highly expressed ECM regulators TIMP1 and TIMP4, which were inhibitors of ECM destruction proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from ECM-related gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation based on known protein functions.

claims.claim: The CHAD+ Ch.1 population is a cluster of chondrocytes that maintain homeostasis in the meniscal tissue.
claims.source: Hence, we inferred that the CHAD+ Ch.1 population is a cluster of chondrocytes that maintain homeostasis in the meniscal tissue.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression and functional analysis.

claims.claim: Ch.3 cells express high levels of PRG4, HTRA1, FN1, CD55, TIMP3, CDON, AMTN.
claims.source: We named another part of this branch that expresses high levels of PRG4, HTRA1, FN1, CD55, TIMP3, CDON, AMTN as Ch.3 (PRG4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claims.claim: Ch.3 cells had lubrication function because the protein proteoglycan 4 (PRG4) has a lubrification function on the articular cartilage surface.
claims.source: We inferred that Ch.3 cells had lubrication function because the protein proteoglycan 4 (PRG4) has a lubrification function on the articular cartilage surface, and these cells were located near the surface of the meniscus.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on PRG4 function and cell localization.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that Ch.3 marker CDON expresses along the surface region of the meniscus.
claims.source: Our immunofluorescence staining further confirmed that its marker CDON expresses along the surface region of the meniscus (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Ch.3 population highly expresses TIMP1/2/3 and may inhibit the matrix decomposition by opposing the MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS family enzymes.
claims.source: This population highly expresses TIMP1/2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and may inhibit the matrix decomposition by opposing the MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS family enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on TIMP expression and known TIMP function.

claims.claim: Ch.2 population highly expresses OA marker genes and chondrocyte hypertrophy genes such as type I, III, and VI collagen genes (COL1A1/2, COL3A1, COL6A1/2/3), POSTN, MMP2, SPARC, and MXRA5.
claims.source: The Ch.2 population highly expresses OA marker genes (Fisch et al., 2018) and chondrocyte hypertrophy genes (Ji et al., 2019) such as type I, III, and VI collagen genes (COL1A1/2, COL3A1, COL6A1/2/3), POSTN, MMP2, SPARC, and MXRA5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: FNDC1 and MXRA5 have been recently reported as signatures of chondrocyte-mediated valve calcification in aortic stenosis.
claims.source: Among these upregulated genes, FNDC1 and MXRA5 have been recently reported as signatures of chondrocyte-mediated valve calcification in aortic stenosis (Bouchareb et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This references findings from Bouchareb et al., 2021.

claims.claim: MXRA5 (matrix remodeling-associated protein 5) is a TGF-β1 regulated gene.
claims.source: It is also known that MXRA5 (matrix remodeling-associated protein 5) is a TGF-β1 regulated gene (Poveda et al., 2017), which is consistent with the high GSVA scores of 'Response to TGFβ' in Ch.2 shown in Figure 2G.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation, consistent with GSVA results.

claims.claim: Ch.2 population expresses MMP, ADAM, and ADAMTS family genes, such as MMP11/13/14, ADAM9/12, and ADAMTS2, which can target collagen, aggrecans or other ECM components.
claims.source: Besides MMP2, this population also expresses other MMP, ADAM, and ADAMTS family genes, such as MMP11/13/14, ADAM9/12, and ADAMTS2, which can target collagen, aggrecans or other ECM components (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation based on known protein functions.

claims.claim: Ch.2 (FNDC1) is a chondrocyte population associated with aberrant ECM degradation and remodeling, and this population may contribute to the progress of human meniscal degeneration.
claims.source: The increased expression of these genes indicated that Ch.2 (FNDC1) is a chondrocyte population associated with aberrant ECM degradation and remodeling, and this population may contribute to the progress of human meniscal degeneration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and functional analysis.

claims.claim: Ch.4 subcluster expresses high levels of CFD, CFH, C1R, C1S, CXCL12, and VCAN.
claims.source: The other CFD+ subcluster in this branch expresses high levels of CFD, CFH, C1R, C1S, CXCL12, and VCAN. We name it Ch.4 (CFD).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claims.claim: Ch.4 subcluster expresses genes associated with alternative complement activation pathways (C1R, C1S, C2, C3, C6, and C7) and may promote inflammation by recruiting macrophages and neutrophils.
claims.source: This subcluster expresses genes associated with alternative complement activation pathways (C1R, C1S, C2, C3, C6, and C7) and may promote inflammation by recruiting macrophages and neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on complement gene expression and known complement functions.

claims.claim: Ch.5 represents chondrocytes in proliferation states and highly expressed S- and G2M-phase cell-cycle genes such as STMN1, CDK1, CENPF, HMGB2, CDKN3, TOP2A.
claims.source: Ch.5 represents chondrocytes in proliferation states. They highly expressed the S- and G2M-phase cell-cycle genes such as STMN1, CDK1, CENPF, HMGB2, CDKN3, TOP2A and were mostly found in the degenerated samples.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claims.claim: 98.63% Ch.5 cells were mapped to Ch.2 and the rest were mapped to Ch.3 using reference mapping analysis.
claims.source: We re-assigned Ch.5 cell identities using cells in Ch.1–Ch.4 clusters as a reference with SingleR (Aran et al., 2019) and found 98.63% Ch.5 cells were mapped to Ch.2 and the rest were mapped to Ch.3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 7F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the reference mapping analysis.

claims.claim: The identity mapping suggested the proliferative Ch.5 could be the origin of the Ch.2 cells increased in the degenerated group.
claims.source: This identity mapping suggested the proliferative Ch.5 could be the origin of the Ch.2 cells increased in the degenerated group.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the reference mapping results.

claims.claim: Genes upregulated in the degeneration group include COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, and ATMN.
claims.source: We identified genes upregulated in the degeneration group, such as COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, and ATMN, and genes upregulated in the normal group, such as APOD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CEBPD, C11orf96, C2orf40 (ECRG4), ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, and MCAM (shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, an extended list of genes in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Genes upregulated in the normal group include APOD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CEBPD, C11orf96, C2orf40 (ECRG4), ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, and MCAM.
claims.source: We identified genes upregulated in the degeneration group, such as COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, and ATMN, and genes upregulated in the normal group, such as APOD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CEBPD, C11orf96, C2orf40 (ECRG4), ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, and MCAM (shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, an extended list of genes in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: The overall expression differences between normal and degenerated conditions are mainly contributed by the cell type compositional changes.
claims.source: We believe the overall expression differences are mainly contributed by the cell type compositional changes because these genes are identified as markers of the chondrocyte subpopulations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between DEGs and cell type markers.

claims.claim: Ch.2 and Ch.3 increased in degeneration while Ch.1 and PCL decreased in degeneration.
claims.source: All these expression differences are consistent with our compositional observations that Ch.2 and Ch.3 increased in degeneration and Ch.1 and PCL decreased in degeneration (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the cell composition analysis.

claims.claim: The overall expressional changes after degeneration could be explained by the increase of Ch.2 and Ch.3 as well as the decrease of PCL cells.
claims.source: Considering all factors above, it appears that the overall expressional changes after degeneration could be explained by the increase of Ch.2 and Ch.3 as well as the decrease of PCL cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference integrating multiple observations.

claims.claim: Ch.2 could have high ECM disassembly scores while Ch.3 could negatively regulate the disassembly regardless of the degeneration states.
claims.source: We first analyzed the GSVA scores of ECM-related gene ontology terms in Figure 3C and found Ch.2 could have high ECM disassembly scores while Ch.3 could negatively regulate the disassembly regardless of the degeneration states.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Ch.2 and Ch.3 got high scores in leukocyte chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and chondrocyte hypertrophy-associated terms.
claims.source: Ch.2 and Ch.3 also got high scores in leukocyte chemotaxis (Figure 3D), angiogenesis (Figure 3E), and chondrocyte hypertrophy-associated terms (Figure 3F); while in contrast, Ch.1 had relatively lower scores on these terms.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: Ch.5 got high scores on the cell-cycle-related terms.
claims.source: Ch.5 got high scores on the cell-cycle-related terms (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: PCL cells got higher pro-angiogenesis scores in degenerated samples than in normal samples.
claims.source: PCL cells got higher pro-angiogenesis scores in degenerated samples than in normal samples.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis comparing conditions.

claims.claim: The inner zone chondrocytes shift from the Ch.1 positions to the Ch.3 positions after degeneration.
claims.source: From the cell density plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A, B, we found that the inner zone chondrocytes shift from the Ch.1 positions to the Ch.3 positions, while the outer zone chondrocytes shift to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cell density analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: The outer zone chondrocytes shift to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions after degeneration.
claims.source: From the cell density plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A, B, we found that the inner zone chondrocytes shift from the Ch.1 positions to the Ch.3 positions, while the outer zone chondrocytes shift to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cell density analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: The outer-degenerated groups consistently got significantly higher inflammation scores than the outer-normal group.
claims.source: We also evaluated the GSVA scores of three inflammation gene sets on the chondrocytes and found the outer-degenerated groups consistently got significantly higher inflammation scores than the outer-normal group. In contrast, the inner zone cells did not have this trend (Figure 3—figure supplement 7E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis of inflammation gene sets shown in figures.

claims.claim: Outer menisci could contribute more to joint inflammation in OA.
claims.source: From the computational analyses, we inferred that outer menisci could contribute more to joint inflammation in OA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the inflammation score analysis.

claims.claim: CDON+ chondrocytes were mainly distributed on the surface of the meniscus tissue.
claims.source: From the staining results, we can clearly find that CDON + chondrocytes were mainly distributed on the surface of the meniscus tissue, and ACTA2+ pericytes were presented surrounding blood vessels.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: ACTA2+ pericytes were presented surrounding blood vessels.
claims.source: From the staining results, we can clearly find that CDON + chondrocytes were mainly distributed on the surface of the meniscus tissue, and ACTA2+ pericytes were presented surrounding blood vessels.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: SERPINA1+, CYP1B1+, and MMP14+ chondrocytes were mixed and scattered inside the meniscus.
claims.source: SERPINA1+, CYP1B1+, and MMP14+ chondrocytes were mixed and scattered inside the meniscus.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments.

claims.claim: Immune cells were mainly distributed around the blood vessels in the meniscus.
claims.source: Immune cells were mainly distributed around the blood vessels in the meniscus.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments.

claims.claim: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased in degenerative specimens.
claims.source: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased, the number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased, and the number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens (Figure 4A–H).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining comparing normal and degenerated samples.

claims.claim: The number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased in degenerative specimens.
claims.source: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased, the number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased, and the number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens (Figure 4A–H).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining comparing normal and degenerated samples.

claims.claim: The number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens.
claims.source: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased, the number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased, and the number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens (Figure 4A–H).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining comparing normal and degenerated samples.

claims.claim: Macrophages/monocytes, neutrophils, mast cells, dendritic cells, T cells, and cycling immune cells were identified in normal and degenerated meniscal samples.
claims.source: For the leukocyte part, we identified macrophages/monocytes, neutrophils, mast cells, dendritic cells, T cells, and cycling immune cells in normal and degenerated meniscal samples (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from immune cell profiling.

claims.claim: Macrophage/monocyte makes up the largest portion of the total immune population.
claims.source: Macrophage/monocyte makes up the largest portion of the total immune population.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immune cell composition analysis.

claims.claim: The percentages of macrophage/monocyte, T cell, dendritic cell, and total immune cell increased in the degeneration group.
claims.source: The percentages of macrophage/monocyte, T cell, dendritic cell, and total immune cell increased in the degeneration group, which was consistent with the vascularization and the damage-induced inflammation (Figure 5B, C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from immune cell composition analysis.

claims.claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL15, and IL18 were upregulated in the cycling immune cell subpopulation in degeneration samples.
claims.source: We noticed some pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes upregulated in degeneration samples, for example, interleukin genes IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL15, and IL18 upregulated in the cycling subpopulation (Figure 5A); chemokine genes CXCL1, CCL3, and CXCL3 upregulated in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claims.claim: Chemokine genes CXCL1, CCL3, and CXCL3 were upregulated in macrophages/monocytes in degeneration samples.
claims.source: We noticed some pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes upregulated in degeneration samples, for example, interleukin genes IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL15, and IL18 upregulated in the cycling subpopulation (Figure 5A); chemokine genes CXCL1, CCL3, and CXCL3 upregulated in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claims.claim: Increased expressions of metallothionein genes MT1X and MT1G were observed in macrophages/monocytes in the degenerated group.
claims.source: We also noticed increased expressions of metallothionein genes in the degenerated group, for example, MT1X and MT1G in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), MT1X, MT2A, and MT1E in T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claims.claim: Increased expressions of metallothionein genes MT1X, MT2A, and MT1E were observed in T cells in the degenerated group.
claims.source: We also noticed increased expressions of metallothionein genes in the degenerated group, for example, MT1X and MT1G in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), MT1X, MT2A, and MT1E in T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claims.claim: An arterial–capillary–venous gradient was identified in the meniscal endothelial cell population.
claims.source: We identified an arterial–capillary–venous gradient in the meniscal endothelial cell population (Figure 5E–G) with other organs' endothelial markers (Schupp et al., 2021; Kalucka et al., 2020).

results.result: The authors generated a single-cell RNA-seq atlas of 45,744 cells from 12 meniscus samples (inner and outer zones) from 8 patients (4 normal, 4 degenerated with OA). The workflow included tissue dissociation, 10× Genomics sequencing, comprehensive quality control (ambient RNA correction with SoupX, doublet removal with DoubletFinder, dissociation score filtering), and batch correction with Harmony.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15, C18-C31, and C42 collectively describe a well-documented experimental workflow with appropriate quality control steps. The methods are standard for scRNA-seq studies, software versions are specified, and the final cell count after QC is reported. The multi-step QC approach (ambient RNA, doublets, dissociation effects, batch correction) is rigorous.

results.result: Five major cell types were identified in inner menisci (chondrocytes, lymphocytes, myeloid cells, endothelial cells, ACTA2+ cells), with outer menisci containing these five plus Schwann cells. Outer menisci showed higher cell type diversity, and degenerated samples had higher immune cell ratios and lower ACTA2+ cell ratios. Cell types were defined by canonical marker expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C43-C50 describe cell type identification using established markers (DCN/PRG4/COL genes for chondrocytes, PLVAP/PECAM1 for endothelial, PTPRC/CD68 for immune, ACTA2 for pericyte-like cells). The compositional differences between inner/outer and normal/degenerated are supported by figures showing cell percentages and UMAP visualizations. The identification of ACTA2+ cells as a distinct population is novel and well-characterized.

results.result: A hierarchical classification identified five chondrocyte subtypes (Ch.1-Ch.5) and two pericyte-like cell (PCL) subtypes (PCL.1 and PCL.2). Chondrocytes express fibroblast markers (DCN, LUM) while PCL cells express smooth muscle/pericyte markers (ACTA2, TAGLN, MYL9). Gene set enrichment analysis confirmed PCL cells have distinct molecular identity from chondrocytes, with enrichment for muscle contraction and smooth muscle cell proliferation terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C51-C54, C57, C67 describe a novel hierarchical cell classification supported by marker gene expression (Figure 2), GSEA results (Figure 2—supplement 2F), and differential expression analysis. The distinction between chondrocyte and PCL populations is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including marker expression, functional enrichment, and GRN analysis. The identification of PCL subtypes with differential inflammatory responses (PCL.1) vs. contractility (PCL.2) is supported by GSVA.

results.result: PCL cells were characterized as pericyte-like based on ACTA2/TAGLN/MYL9 expression, perivascular localization (confirmed by immunofluorescence), enrichment in vascularized outer meniscus, and comparison to similar cells in intervertebral disc. PCL cells showed weak differentiation potential into degenerated progenitors (DegP) and expressed anti-angiogenic collagen fragments (COL4A1/2, COL18A1). The authors acknowledge difficulty distinguishing pericytes from smooth muscle cells transcriptomically.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C66 provide converging evidence for PCL identity: marker expression consistent with pericytes across multiple organs (C56, C62), spatial localization around blood vessels (C61, immunofluorescence in Figure 4), functional gene expression (C66, anti-angiogenic collagens), and appropriate caveats about transcriptomic limitations (C63). The comparison to Sun et al. 2020 (C58-C59) strengthens the characterization by distinguishing PCL from FCP based on lack of DegP marker expression.

results.result: Ch.1 (CHAD+) is the largest chondrocyte population, expressing CHI3L1/2 (RegC markers), TIMP1/4 (ECM protease inhibitors), and showing anti-angiogenesis activity by GSVA. This population decreased in degeneration and is inferred to maintain meniscal homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 characterize Ch.1 with marker expression (CHAD, CHI3L1/2, TIMP1/4), functional inference from GSVA (anti-angiogenesis, Figure 2G), compositional changes (decreased in degeneration, Figure 3B), and literature support for CHI3L1/2 as RegC markers (C72). The homeostasis inference (C76) is reasonable given TIMP expression and anti-angiogenic function, though it remains an inference rather than direct functional validation.

results.result: Ch.3 (PRG4+) expresses surface markers (PRG4, CDON, CD55, TIMP3, AMTN) and is localized to the meniscus surface by immunofluorescence. This population is inferred to have lubrication function based on PRG4's known role in articular cartilage and may inhibit matrix decomposition via TIMP1/2/3 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 characterize Ch.3 with marker expression and spatial validation. The surface localization of CDON+ cells is directly confirmed by immunofluorescence (C79, Figure 4C-D). The lubrication function inference (C78) is reasonable given PRG4's established role and surface localization, though functional validation is lacking. TIMP expression (C80) supports anti-degradative function.

results.result: Ch.2 (FNDC1+) highly expresses OA markers and hypertrophy genes (COL1A1/2, COL3A1, COL6A1/2/3, POSTN, MMP2, SPARC, MXRA5, FNDC1) and matrix-degrading enzymes (MMP11/13/14, ADAM9/12, ADAMTS2). This population is associated with aberrant ECM degradation and remodeling and may contribute to meniscal degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 characterize Ch.2 as a degenerative population with extensive gene expression evidence (Figure 3—supplement 2A,B) and literature support for FNDC1/MXRA5 in calcification (C82) and MXRA5 as TGF-β regulated (C83, consistent with GSVA). The expression of multiple MMPs/ADAMs/ADAMTS (C84) strongly supports the ECM degradation inference (C85). The conclusion that Ch.2 contributes to degeneration is well-supported by marker expression and functional enrichment.

results.result: Ch.4 (CFD+) expresses complement pathway genes (C1R, C1S, C2, C3, C6, C7, CFD, CFH) and chemokine CXCL12, and may promote inflammation by recruiting macrophages and neutrophils.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 characterize Ch.4 with complement gene expression (Figure 3—supplement 1C) and infer inflammatory function based on known complement biology. The inference about immune cell recruitment (C87) is reasonable given complement's established role in inflammation, though direct functional validation is absent.

results.result: Ch.5 represents proliferating chondrocytes expressing S/G2M cell cycle genes (STMN1, CDK1, CENPF, HMGB2, CDKN3, TOP2A), found mostly in degenerated samples. Reference mapping showed 98.63% of Ch.5 cells mapped to Ch.2, suggesting Ch.5 could be the origin of increased Ch.2 cells in degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 characterize Ch.5 with cell cycle marker expression and use reference mapping (SingleR) to infer lineage relationships. The mapping result (C89, 98.63% to Ch.2) is quantitative and supports the inference that proliferating Ch.5 gives rise to Ch.2 (C90). However, this remains correlative; lineage tracing would be needed for definitive proof. The inference is reasonable but should be stated as a hypothesis.

results.result: Differential expression analysis between normal and degenerated conditions identified genes upregulated in degeneration (COL1A1/2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, ATMN) and normal (APOD, CHI3L1/2, CEBPD, ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, MCAM). These differences are attributed mainly to cell type compositional changes (Ch.2/Ch.3 increase, Ch.1/PCL decrease in degeneration).
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 describe DEG analysis with the key insight that bulk expression differences reflect compositional changes rather than within-cell-type changes. This is well-supported by showing that DEGs correspond to cell type markers (C93) and that compositional shifts match expression patterns (C94-C95, Figure 3A-B). This is an important analytical insight that properly attributes expression changes to cell composition.

results.result: GSVA analysis revealed functional differences between chondrocyte subtypes: Ch.2 had high ECM disassembly scores while Ch.3 negatively regulated disassembly; Ch.2 and Ch.3 scored high for leukocyte chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and chondrocyte hypertrophy; Ch.5 scored high for cell cycle terms; PCL cells had higher pro-angiogenesis scores in degenerated samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 describe GSVA results (Figure 3C-F) that assign functional profiles to cell subtypes. The analysis is appropriate for inferring cell functions from gene expression, though GSVA scores represent potential rather than demonstrated activity. The results are internally consistent with marker expression patterns (e.g., Ch.2 expressing MMPs and scoring high for ECM disassembly).

results.result: Cell density analysis showed zonation-specific shifts in degeneration: inner zone chondrocytes shifted from Ch.1 to Ch.3 positions, while outer zone chondrocytes shifted to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions. Outer-degenerated samples had significantly higher inflammation scores than outer-normal, leading to the inference that outer menisci contribute more to joint inflammation in OA.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 describe zonation-dependent changes using cell density plots (Figure 3—supplement 7A,B) and GSVA inflammation scores (Figure 3—supplement 7E). The statistical comparison of inflammation scores between outer-degenerated and outer-normal is quantitative with p-values. The inference about outer menisci contributing more to OA inflammation (C103) is reasonable given the data, though it remains an inference from transcriptional profiles rather than direct measurement of inflammatory mediators.

results.result: Immunofluorescence staining validated spatial distributions: CDON+ chondrocytes (Ch.3) on meniscus surface, ACTA2+ pericytes surrounding blood vessels, SERPINA1+/CYP1B1+/MMP14+ chondrocytes scattered inside, and immune cells around blood vessels. Degenerated specimens showed decreased ACTA2+ cells, increased MMP14+ chondrocytes, and increased vascular endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110 describe immunofluorescence validation (Figure 4) that confirms scRNA-seq predictions about cell localization and compositional changes. The spatial validation of CDON (surface), ACTA2 (perivascular), and immune cells (perivascular) strengthens the scRNA-seq findings. The quantitative changes in degeneration (decreased ACTA2+, increased MMP14+, increased endothelial) are visually apparent in the images and consistent with scRNA-seq compositional analysis.

results.result: Immune cell profiling identified macrophages/monocytes (largest population), neutrophils, mast cells, dendritic cells, T cells, and cycling immune cells. Degeneration was associated with increased percentages of macrophages/monocytes, T cells, dendritic cells, and total immune cells, along with upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL1A/B, IL6, IL15, IL18 in cycling cells; CXCL1, CCL3, CXCL3 in macrophages) and metallothionein genes (MT1X, MT1G, MT2A, MT1E).
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C117 characterize immune cell populations and their changes in degeneration using standard markers (Figure 5A-C, Figure 5—supplement 1). The compositional increases in degeneration are quantified with error bars (Figure 5D). The upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (C114-C115) is shown in figures and consistent with damage-induced inflammation. Metallothionein upregulation (C116-C117) is an interesting observation, though its functional significance is not explored.

results.result: Endothelial cell analysis identified an arterial-capillary-venous gradient using markers from other organs (GJA5 for capillary-arterial, PLVAP for capillary, VWF for capillary-venous), plus a small population of lymphatic endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 describe endothelial cell subtyping (Figure 5E-G) using established markers from other tissues (C118, citing Schupp et al. 2021 and Kalucka et al. 2020). The identification of arterial-capillary-venous gradient is appropriate given marker expression patterns. The lymphatic endothelial cell observation (C122) is noted as a small cluster with appropriate uncertainty about its origin.

results.result: Endothelial cell DEG analysis showed upregulation of CST3, ACKR1, RBP7, IGFBP4 in normal samples and S100A4, DDIT4, CRIP1, MGP in degenerated samples. CST3 (top normal DEG) inhibits endothelial cell proliferation, migration, tube formation, and permeability; ACKR1 encodes a chemokine decoy receptor that inhibits chemokine effectiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 describe endothelial DEGs (Figure 5H) with functional interpretation supported by literature (C125-C126). The upregulation of anti-angiogenic/anti-chemotactic factors (CST3, ACKR1) in normal samples is consistent with the overall model of vascular stability in health. The functional interpretations are based on cited literature rather than experiments in this study.

results.result: Cell-cell interaction analysis showed generally increased CCI intensities in degeneration, especially for endothelial and immune cells. Specific enhanced interactions included CXCL8-SDC2 (immune to chondrocytes/PCL), CALM1/2-INSR (multiple cell types to endothelial, pro-angiogenic), and immunoregulatory interactions via TNF superfamily, TGF superfamily, and HLA-APLP2.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 describe computational CCI analysis (Figure 5I-J, Figure 5—supplement 2) using ligand-receptor databases. The general increase in CCI intensity in degeneration (C127) is shown in Figure 5I. Specific examples (C128-C130) are supported by expression data and literature (C129 cites Walker et al. 2021 for INSR pro-angiogenic function). However, the authors appropriately note these are computational predictions not experimentally validated.

results.result: The authors propose that in normal meniscus, ECM synthesis and disassembly are balanced, with Ch.1 maintaining balance via TIMP expression, PCL cells maintaining vascular stability, and ACKR1 attenuating angiogenesis by neutralizing chemokines.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 synthesize observations into a homeostasis model. The inferences are reasonable given: Ch.1 expresses TIMPs and is decreased in degeneration (C132), PCL cells are perivascular and decreased in degeneration (C133), and ACKR1 is upregulated in normal endothelial cells (C134). However, these remain inferences from expression data and compositional changes rather than functional validation. The model is plausible but requires experimental testing.

results.result: The authors propose that in degenerated meniscus, Ch.2/Ch.3 expression of ECM decomposers (MMPs/ADAMs/ADAMTS) surpasses TIMP inhibition, leading to ECM breakdown. Blood vessels have a dual role: helping restore acute injuries but also providing pathways for immune cell infiltration and inflammation. Pericyte detachment and decrease may lead to pathological states.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 propose a degeneration mechanism based on observed changes: increased Ch.2/Ch.3 with high MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS expression, increased vascularization, increased immune infiltration, and decreased PCL cells. The model is internally consistent with the data and supported by literature on pericyte function (C137 cites three papers). However, the causal relationships remain inferential; the study is descriptive/correlative rather than mechanistic.

results.result: The authors hypothesize loop-like interactions among ECM disassembly, angiogenesis, and inflammation driving meniscal degeneration, and suggest that changing chondrocyte subtype ratios and limiting blood vessel proliferation may delay or reverse degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C138 propose a positive feedback loop model and therapeutic implications. While the model is consistent with observed correlations (increased Ch.2/Ch.3, angiogenesis, immune infiltration, ECM degradation all co-occur), the study does not demonstrate causal loop-like interactions or test interventions. The therapeutic suggestion (C138) is speculative. The model is a reasonable hypothesis requiring experimental validation through perturbation studies, time-course analysis, or functional experiments.

results.result: PCL.1 and PCL.2 subtypes show functional differences: PCL.1 had more active responses to IL-1 and TNF-α and expressed higher chemokines (CCL2, CCL19, CCL21, CXCL12) and COL4A1/2; PCL.2 had higher myofibril gene set activation scores, suggesting higher muscle contractility and potential blood flow regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 characterize PCL subtypes using GSVA (Figure 2G) and gene expression (Figure 3—supplement 1D,E). The functional inferences are reasonable given gene expression patterns and supported by literature (C70 cites van Dijk et al. 2015 on contractility). The distinction between inflammatory-responsive (PCL.1) and contractile (PCL.2) subtypes is well-supported by multiple gene expression patterns.

results.result: The analysis pipeline included MetaCell for noise reduction and data consistency, HGC for hierarchical relationships, Seurat for DEG identification, clusterProfiler for enrichment analysis with BH-adjusted p<0.05, GSVA for gene set activity scores, and pySCENIC for gene regulatory network inference.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 describe the computational analysis pipeline using established methods. Each tool is appropriately cited and used for its intended purpose. The p-value threshold (0.05 BH-adjusted, C36) is standard. The combination of methods (metacells for noise reduction, hierarchical clustering, DEG analysis, enrichment, GSVA, GRN) provides multiple complementary views of the data. The methods are appropriate and well-documented.

results.result: The study acknowledges that females make up the majority of donors (since OA is more common in middle-aged/older females), and the cellular profiles may better represent the female population.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 acknowledge a study limitation regarding sex bias in the donor population. This is an appropriate caveat about generalizability. The explanation for the bias (OA prevalence in females) is reasonable, though it doesn't eliminate the limitation. The acknowledgment of this limitation is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The authors speculate that cellular and molecular mechanisms observed in meniscal degeneration (angiogenesis, inflammation) could apply to intervertebral disc and articular cartilage degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 is explicitly speculative. While the tissues share some features (cartilaginous, similar cell types, ECM composition), the generalization requires validation in those tissues. The speculation is reasonable given similarities but remains untested. This is appropriately framed as speculation rather than a conclusion.

results.result: The introduction establishes background knowledge: meniscus degeneration is a major origin of knee OA; nearly half of patients with meniscal degeneration develop OA; inflammatory responses and biomineralization affect the meniscus microenvironment; the meniscus has anatomical zonation (inner white-white vs. outer red-red) with different vascularization, collagen composition, PG content, and healing capacity; and prior studies have characterized meniscal cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C14 provide background context supported by citations. These are established facts from prior literature (C5-C6, C11-C14 cite specific papers) or anatomical knowledge (C7-C10). The background appropriately sets up the study's rationale. No evaluation of novel findings is needed for these contextual claims.

results.result: The study identified new chondrocyte subtypes associated with degeneration and observed damage-induced inflammatory responses in degenerated samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C17 are high-level summary statements of major findings. C3 (new chondrocyte subtypes) is supported by the detailed characterization of Ch.1-Ch.5 with novel markers and functions. C17 (damage-induced inflammatory responses) is supported by immune cell profiling showing increased immune cells and pro-inflammatory cytokines in degeneration. These summary claims accurately reflect the detailed findings.

results.result: Background on pericyte/smooth muscle cell markers and functions: ACTA2 encodes smooth muscle actin for vascular contractility; ACTA2/TAGLN/MYH/MYL genes identify pericytes/smooth muscle cells across organs; pericytes are difficult to distinguish from smooth muscle cells transcriptomically; pericytes attach to endothelial cells and maintain vascular stability; pericytes have pro-angiogenesis capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56, C63-C65 provide background knowledge about pericytes supported by multiple citations. These establish the rationale for naming the ACTA2+ population as pericyte-like cells and interpreting their function. The acknowledgment of difficulty distinguishing pericytes from smooth muscle cells (C63) is an important caveat supported by literature.

results.result: Morphological examination showed normal meniscal specimens are smooth and complete with clear structure, while degenerated specimens are swollen, irregular, structurally damaged, and vascularized.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 describe gross morphological observations from specimen photographs (Figure 1A). These are straightforward visual observations that establish the phenotypic differences between normal and degenerated samples. The observations are consistent with expected OA pathology.

results.result: Literature support for gene functions: Kumar et al. 2017 analyzed FABP4/RGS5/MYH11/MYH9/CNN1/TAGLN in pericyte/smooth muscle cell specification; Ji et al. 2019 described CHI3L1/2 as RegC markers; Bouchareb et al. 2021 reported FNDC1/MXRA5 in valve calcification; Poveda et al. 2017 showed MXRA5 is TGF-β1 regulated; Li et al. 2018 reported CST3 inhibits endothelial cell functions; Rot 2005 described ACKR1 as chemokine decoy receptor.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C72, C82-C83, C125-C126 cite specific papers to support functional interpretations of genes identified in the study. These citations are appropriate and strengthen the functional inferences. The cited papers are relevant to the genes and functions discussed. This represents appropriate use of literature to interpret findings.
